newsitem.title: UK: Octuplet miscarriage sparks calls for new UK laws.
newsitem.headline: Octuplet miscarriage sparks calls for new UK laws.

text.p: The case of a British woman who ignored doctors' advice and tried unsuccessfully to give birth to octuplets brought calls on Thursday for tighter laws on who should be given fertility treatment.

Mandy Allwood, 31, lost three of her babies in the 19th week of her pregnancy on Monday and the remaining five on Wednesday. The case received wide publicity after she sold her story to a Sunday tabloid newspaper.
Publicist Max Clifford said the dead foetuses, six boys and two girls, were laid in a cot beside Allwood's bed, with pink and blue tags according to their sex.
Critics expressed some sympathy for Allwood but said doctors had been irresponsible to treat a woman who already had a child and took fertility drugs in a bid to save a rocky relationship.
"Is it an act of responsibility to offer fertility treatments with such promiscuity to people who are plainly ill-suited to receive them?" asked the London Evening Standard.

"If (doctors) are to continue to enjoy the respect they have long commanded...it is not enough for some of them to merely prescribe or cut, while shrugging from behind the mask: "The morals is nothing to do with me, guv.'"
Clifford said Allwood had spent a restless night but did not regret her decision to ignore doctors' advice that some of the foetuses should be aborted to give the rest a chance.
Dr Robert Forman, clinical director of the London Gynaecological and Fertility Centre, said the case had brought up many issues regarding access to fertility treatment.

"I think the doctors have their share of responsibility but the patients also have a responsibility. If there's one lesson to be learned from this it's that both have to work in partnership," he said.
About 18,000 women a year are treated at British fertility clinics, which are attracting increasing attention as the result of several high-profile cases this year.
Nicholas Coote, assistant general secretary of the Catholic Bishops' Conference, said doctors should draw up new guidelines and suggested only married couples should be treated.

"This (would) provide a very clear line...which stops you having some less clear distinction which appears to discriminate against a person on very personal grounds or on very private grounds," he told BBC Radio.
Some commentators contrasted the Allwood affair with that of a 30-year-old widow now fighting for the right to be impregnated with her dead husband's sperm.
The Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority refused permission for her artificial insemination, saying the law would be broken as she did not have her husband's written consent.
The authority provoked uproar in July when it ordered the destruction of thousands of human foetuses created by in-vitro fertilisation because they had passed a legal deadline.
Doctors came under attack the same month for agreeing to abort one of a pair of foetuses after the mother said she could only afford one child.

Baroness Helen Warnock, author of a 1987 report which formed the framework of current laws on fertility treatment, said doctors should have the right to carry out selective abortions in cases where multiple births were expected.
"A rule that only married couples (would receive treatment) would probably lead to a lot of marriages of convenience which then wouldn't come to anything," she told BBC Radio.
